British Classic Gets Unexpected Second Chance After 37 Years in the Bushes, Agrees To Run
10 photos
Photo: UK Barn Finds/YouTube
When it comes to British classics, we often get excited about Jaguars, Aston Martins , Rolls-Royces, and Bentleys. And that makes sense; petrolheads have a thing for sports cars and luxury vehicles. But needless to say, the original Mini Cooper also has a cult following.
However, the British automotive heritage extends far beyond the aforementioned brands and nameplates. We also have old Land Rovers, as well as carmakers like Lotus, Triumph, and MG. The Elan, TR6, and MGB definitely deserve spots in the automotive hall of fame, as do the Ford Cortina and Escort. However, some cars don't get as much attention as they should outside the UK. The Morris Minor is one of them.
The Minor was produced by Morris Motors Limited, which was established in 1919. The company merged with Austin to form the British Motor Corporation (BMC) in 1952, but the Morris name remained in use until 1984. Designed by Alec Issigonis, who also penned the Mini Cooper, the Minor is the company's most famous car.
The Morris Minor debuted in 1948, replacing the Eight. It was one of Britain's first post-WW2 designs. Measuring only 148 inches (3,759 mm) long, the Minor arrived with features that were ahead of their time for an economy car, including rack-and-pinion steering and independent suspension. Its low price and affordable maintenance made it quite popular in post-war Britain.
Morris sold one million units by late 1960 and a total of 1.6 million examples until the nameplate was discontinued in 1971. Body styles included a two-door sedan, a four-door sedan, a two-door convertible, and a two-door wagon. The Minor received notable upgrades in 1952, 1956, and 1962. All cars were powered by small-displacement four-cylinder engines.
Despite the massive production number, the Morris Minor is a rare sight today. How so? Well, for starters, it was treated as a throw-away vehicle; most Minors were dumped into junkyards. Second, these cars aren't worth much today, so fully restored vehicles aren't common outside the Morris Minor fan club.
And sadly enough, very few Minors get rescued nowadays. Most of them have become rust buckets and barely provide useful parts for ongoing projects. The example you see here is one of the many Minors that sat for decades, but unlike its siblings, it's still (mostly) in one piece. And it was also lucky enough to get a revival.
The car had been parked in a backyard in 1989, and it almost became one with the bushes in 37 years. Our host says that the rescue was unintentional; the Morris was purchased only because it came as a package deal with another vehicle he wanted from the property. Fortunately, that didn't stop the buyer from cleaning it and getting the engine running again.
And while the car looked damaged beyond salvation, the old inline-four agreed to run again without much intervention. And amazingly enough, it was still capable of moving the Minor around. The car is obviously too rusty to be revived with reasonable costs, but it's cool to see it driving after so many decades off the road.
This Minor is a Series III, also known as the Minor 1000 . This version debuted in 1956 and remained in production until 1971, with nearly 850,000 units made. How can you tell it apart from older Minors? Well, the front grille is the obvious hint; it's wider at the top and has horizontal slats. Hit the play button below to see it coming back to life.
